sections.Kurzabstract: The KSE is an adaptation of the American original and measures loneliness with 20 items. Reliability: Internal consistency according to Cronbach's alpha and split-half reliability were .88; stability after a 3-month interval was rtt = .72. Validity: The KSE was correlated with the FPI-K and a shyness scale as well as with several constructs such as life situation, physical attractiveness and causal attribution.
sections.Diagnostische Zielsetzung: The KSE serves the quantitative assessment of loneliness in adults.
sections.Aufbau: The scale consists of a total of 20 items, half of which are worded negatively.
sections.Grundlagen und Konstruktion: The scale is an adaptation of the American original and was psychometrically examined in the German-speaking area, both in student samples and in a clinical subsample.
sections.Empirische Prüfung und Gütekriterien:
Reliability: Internal consistency according to Cronbach's alpha and split-half reliability were .88; stability after a 3-month interval was rtt = .72.
Validity: The KSE was correlated with the FPI-K and a shyness scale as well as with several constructs such as life situation, physical attractiveness and causal attribution.
Norms: The instrument is not normed. Means and standard deviations are available, which were collected in the mid-1980s in student and clinical samples.
sections.Testkonzept/Theoretischer Hintergrund:
The KSE is based on the American loneliness scale developed at the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA), the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale (Russell, Peplau & Cutrona, 1980). The UCLA Loneliness Scale (UCLA-LS) is regarded as the internationally most widely used instrument for measuring loneliness. The KSE is a German version of the UCLA-LS (for further versions of the UCLA-LS see the section "Test forms"). In adults, the scale can be used for the quantitative assessment of loneliness.
The theoretical basis of the KSE is a cognitive-affective discrepancy model of loneliness (cf. Peplau & Perlman, 1982; Stephan & Fäth, 1989). In this model, loneliness is defined as the perception, experienced as unpleasant, of a deficit between the desired and the actual shape of a person's social relationships. Causes and consequences of loneliness are not assessed with the KSE (on the causality of loneliness see Bücker, 2022; Holt-Lunstad et al. 2015; Prosetzky, 2022; Stephan, 1987).
sections.Testkonzept/Testaufbau: The KSE consists of 10 positively worded (example: „Es gibt Menschen, denen ich mich eng verbunden fühle“) and 10 negatively worded (example: „So zurückgezogen wie ich bin, fühle ich mich unglücklich“) items. Participants are to indicate in each case how often they feel the way these statements describe. For this purpose, a four-point response scale with the alternatives „Nie“, „Selten“, „Manchmal“ and „Oft“ is provided.
sections.Testkonzept/Auswertungsmodus: The answers are scored from one point („Nie“) to four points („Oft“). Because the scale is keyed in the direction of high loneliness, the scores for the 10 positively worded items must be reversed for scoring. A person's test score then corresponds to the sum across all 20 items. The numerical range of the KSE is thus between 20 and 80 points.
sections.Testkonzept/Auswertungshilfen:
Scoring by hand is simple. No templates or scoring programs have been developed for it. Norms are available for student samples (see Table 1); current population-representative norms are, to our knowledge, not available.
For the interpretation of KSE means, the respondents' self-ratings are also available (cf. section "Norming") as well as Table 1 with the item statistics (see section "Items").
sections.Durchführung/Testformen:
The KSE can be administered as an individual or group test. Comparability with the American original is high; the quality criteria of the KSE correspond to those of the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale by Russell et al. (1980).
Short versions
Lamm & Stephan (1986, 1987) additionally propose a short form of the KSE consisting of the five items 2, 13, 14, 17 and 18. These items correlate most highly with the direct self-rating of loneliness. The short scale shows sufficient reliability with alpha = .79 and a high correlation with the total scale with r = .91. The distribution statistics of the short scale (distribution shape, central tendency, dispersion, sex differences) also largely correspond to those of the total scale.
In more recent population-representative longitudinal studies in Germany and the USA, a further short scale based on items 2, 11 and 14 is used (Entringer, 2022; Hawkley et al., 2016).
Other German adaptations of the UCLA-LS
Besides the KSE, there are further German versions of the UCLA-LS (Döring & Bortz, 1993; Quast, 1985; Schwab, 1986; Veiel & Herrle, 1989; Windisch & Kniel, 1988). However, these adaptations in part use response scales different from the American original or have not yet been comprehensively validated.
Other American versions of the UCLA-LS
Besides the revised UCLA-LS by Russell et al. (1980), on which the development of the KSE was based, there are two further versions of this scale: The original version by Russell, Peplau and Ferguson (1978) - referred to below as UCLA-LS version 1 - likewise contains 20 items, which, however, were without exception negatively keyed, that is, keyed in the direction of high loneliness. This methodological weakness was corrected in the later versions.
The revised version of this scale, the UCLA-LS version 2 by Russell et al. (1980), contains - like the present German version - 10 negatively and 10 positively keyed items in order to counteract possible response tendencies of the test takers. On a scale from "Never" to "Often", respondents are to indicate how often the respective statement (e.g. "I feel left out") applies to themselves.
The UCLA-LS version 3 by Russell (1996) was intended to simplify the scale linguistically in order to make the items more comprehensible, especially for persons with little test experience. Possible problems of this version are discussed in the section "Evaluation".
sections.Durchführung/Altersbereiche: The scale can be used for the quantitative assessment of loneliness in adolescents aged 14 and older and in adults. For younger age groups, special measurement instruments have been developed (examples are discussed by Cole et al., 2021).
sections.Durchführung/Durchführungszeit: The average administration time for the KSE total scale is 2-6 minutes. No time limit is provided.
sections.Durchführung/Material:
In addition to the present documentation of the instrument, the test package contains a written questionnaire including instructions.
The test can be administered in writing, orally, by telephone, online or by video conference. Corresponding material for the administration of the test must be prepared.
sections.Durchführung/Instruktion:
The standardized instruction is given below (cf. Russell et al., 1980, S. 475):
„Bitte geben Sie an, wie oft Sie sich so fühlen, wie in den nachfolgenden Aussagen beschrieben. Kreisen Sie eine Zahl für jede Aussage ein.“
sections.Durchführung/Durchführungsvoraussetzunge: No special qualification of the test administrator is required.
sections.Testkonstruktion: The KSE is - like the UCLA-LS - conceived as a global and unidimensional measure of loneliness and was constructed according to the principles of classical test theory (cf. Russell et al., 1980). The development of the German scale is described in Lamm & Stephan (1986, 1987). The psychometric properties of the instrument from the perspective of classical as well as probabilistic test theory are discussed by Fäth (1987). In this context it should be mentioned that a loneliness scale explicitly constructed according to probabilistic test theory also exists, the RTLS (Rasch-Type Loneliness Scale; cf. de Jong-Gierveld & Kamphuis, 1985; de Jong-Gierveld & van Tilburg, 2006).
sections.Gütekriterien/Objektivität: Owing to the standardization, the simple calculation and the available reference values, objectivity in administration, scoring and interpretation is largely ensured for the KSE.
sections.Gütekriterien/Reliabilität: The KSE shows sufficient internal consistency: Cronbach's alpha was .88, and the split-half coefficients according to Spearman and Guttman were likewise .88. After a time interval of 3 months, the test-retest reliability was rtt = .72, thus reaching values similar to those of the American original scale (cf. Russell, 1982, 1996).
sections.Gütekriterien/Validität:
To examine the validity of the KSE, the following measurement instruments and criteria, among others, were used: the short version of the Freiburger Persönlichkeitsinventar (FPI-K; Fahrenberg et al., 1978), the shyness scale by Cheek (1979), questions on the respondents' current life situation and satisfaction, self-ratings of physical attractiveness and social skills, as well as the assessment of the causes of one's own feelings of loneliness. Evidence for the convergent validity of the KSE is that loneliness goes along with dissatisfaction with one's own social contacts, low self-rated social skills, dissatisfaction with one's partner (if any), low self-rated attractiveness, low self-esteem and a rather feminine psychological gender. Loneliness is furthermore associated with higher levels of introversion, neuroticism, shyness, depressiveness and psychosomatic disturbance. Evidence for the discriminant validity of the KSE is that there are no relationships between loneliness and the personality factors (spontaneous and reactive) aggressiveness and excitability.
The following table shows the correlations between these constructs and the KSE.

Respondents who had sought help at a psychological counselling centre showed clearly higher loneliness scores (n = 27, M = 49.1) than the non-clinical group (n = 247, M = 33.4; t = 6.35, df = 272, p < .001). Persons who attributed their feelings of loneliness internally-stably also showed strongly elevated loneliness (n = 21, M = 47.9) compared with persons with other attribution patterns (n = 213, M = 33.1; t = 6.73, df = 232, p < .001).
sections.Gütekriterien/Normierung:
The results reported here are based on a sample of N = 247 students at a West German university. These persons came from different departments and semesters of study and were asked to participate in the study in courses in the winter semester 1986/87. The mean age of the students was 23.2 years; about 41 percent were female. To examine stability, some of the test persons (N = 97) completed the KSE again three months later.
In this group, which is considerably younger, more highly educated and sociologically more homogeneous than the general population, loneliness is rather low (M = 33.4, Min = 20, Max = 67, SD = 8.8). The raw score distribution is left-steep (Md = 32.0, skewness = 1.32), narrow-peaked (excess = 1.98) and deviates significantly from a normal distribution (KS-Z = 2.19, p < .01). Male respondents showed slightly (but not significantly) higher means than female respondents (MM = 34.1 vs. MF = 32.3), which confirms earlier findings in American students (Russell et al., 1980, S. 477) and German students (Lamm & Stephan, 1986, S. 131).
Despite the low loneliness overall among students, the data suggest that almost one in six in this group experiences loneliness as a problem. In the direct self-ratings of loneliness, about 16 percent of respondents state that they are lonely "fast immer", "sehr häufig" or "einigermaßen häufig". This corresponds to a KSE total score of 45 points or more, as Table 3 shows.

Current norms for the German general population are currently not available; corresponding surveys with the KSE are being planned.
sections.Anwendungsmöglichkeiten:
The KSE can preferably be used in sociological, psychological, educational and medical research, and also in clinical diagnostics, monitoring of treatment outcome and personality assessment. Further fields of application would be:
Monitoring of loneliness within population-representative longitudinal studies with suitable short scales (e.g. Entringer, 2022; Mund, 2022)
Conducting internationally comparative studies on changes in loneliness and on the evaluation of interventions against loneliness
Identification of problem groups in the population (marginal groups and minorities, children, older people, people living alone, hospitalized persons, persons with a direct migration background, low education and/or low income)
Studies on the impact of external shocks on the loneliness of affected groups (epidemics, economic crises, natural disasters, war, flight, displacement, etc.)
sections.Bewertung:
With the KSE, an adaptation of the UCLA-LS that is reliable and valid according to the quality criteria of classical test theory is available. The internal consistency, temporal stability and construct validity of the scale found in American studies could be confirmed. The latter is remarkable insofar as the relevant personality constructs were naturally assessed with other measurement instruments and yet very similar correlations were found as in the American original studies.
As a limitation, it should be noted that the results are based on a student sample that not only differs strongly from the general population in terms of age, economic and sociological characteristics, but is also considerably more homogeneous with regard to these criteria. No disadvantage for the applicability of the KSE in heterogeneous groups or in the general population results from this. The quality criteria of the KSE in such groups are rather underestimated than overestimated by using a student study sample, as Stephan & Fäth (1989, S. 163) have shown.
Versions of the UCLA-LS
The revisions of the UCLA-LS listed in the section "Test forms" are not consistently to be evaluated positively. The UCLA-LS version 3 by Russell (1996) does contain linguistic simplifications to increase the comprehensibility of the items, especially for older persons and persons with a low level of education. For example, one item (# 4) was reverse-keyed to avoid double negatives; the new scale consequently contains 9 positively and 11 negatively keyed items. In addition, however, both the question format and the response format were changed for all items. All items now begin with the phrase "How often do you feel …", and the given response categories run from "Never" to "Always" (instead of "Often" as in the previous version 2). In particular the two last-mentioned changes considerably impede the comparability of research results obtained with versions 2 and 3. A possible further disadvantage of the UCLA-LS version 3 is its monotonous question format, which might have a tiring and demotivating effect on some test persons. Depending on the research question and target group, version 2 would thus be preferable to version 3.
Dimensionality of the scale
Since the early 1980s, the dimensionality of the UCLA-LS has been discussed controversially (Russell, 1982). This discussion continues to the present day (Mund, 2022; Mund et al., 2023). Confirmatory factor analyses by Russell (1996) suggest the assumption of a single bipolar loneliness factor as well as of two method factors reflecting the keying of the items (negative vs. positive).
Other loneliness scales, in contrast, are explicitly conceived as multidimensional. These include the RTLS already mentioned in the section "Test construction" as well as the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale for Adults (SELSA; DiTommaso & Spinner, 1993) and the Differential Loneliness Scale (DLS; Schmidt & Sermat, 1983). These scales take up the distinction between emotional and social loneliness based on Weiss (1973) and in part differentiate further according to different areas of life (intimate relationships, family, circle of friends, larger communities, society as a whole).

Respondents who had sought help at a psychological counselling centre showed clearly higher loneliness scores (n = 27, M = 49.1) than the non-clinical group (n = 247, M = 33.4; t = 6.35, df = 272, p < .001). Persons who attributed their feelings of loneliness internally-stably also showed strongly elevated loneliness (n = 21, M = 47.9) compared with persons with other attribution patterns (n = 213, M = 33.1; t = 6.73, df = 232, p < .001).
Study.Norming:
The results reported here are based on a sample of N = 247 students at a West German university. These persons came from different departments and semesters of study and were asked to participate in the study in courses in the winter semester 1986/87. The mean age of the students was 23.2 years; about 41 percent were female. To examine stability, some of the test persons (N = 97) completed the KSE again three months later.
In this group, which is considerably younger, more highly educated and sociologically more homogeneous than the general population, loneliness is rather low (M = 33.4, Min = 20, Max = 67, SD = 8.8). The raw score distribution is left-steep (Md = 32.0, skewness = 1.32), narrow-peaked (excess = 1.98) and deviates significantly from a normal distribution (KS-Z = 2.19, p < .01). Male respondents showed slightly (but not significantly) higher means than female respondents (MM = 34.1 vs. MF = 32.3), which confirms earlier findings in American students (Russell et al., 1980, S. 477) and German students (Lamm & Stephan, 1986, S. 131).
Despite the low loneliness overall among students, the data suggest that almost one in six in this group experiences loneliness as a problem. In the direct self-ratings of loneliness, about 16 percent of respondents state that they are lonely "fast immer", "sehr häufig" or "einigermaßen häufig". This corresponds to a KSE total score of 45 points or more, as Table 3 shows.
